title: What Is a Hiring Manager? Role, Duties, and Responsibilities October 2026
summary: Understand the hiring manager job description for October 2026, covering duties, pay benchmarks, and interview responsibilities.
body_markdown:
A role opens, and the founder assumes the recruiter is writing the criteria, the recruiter assumes the team lead already defined them, and the team lead assumes someone will flag it if the scope is wrong. Nobody owns the call until a candidate is sitting in front of three people who can’t agree on what they’re actually screening for. Getting the split right lets you hire faster with fewer repeat interviews and clearer ownership of who decides what, but most teams only sort this out after a bad hire forces the conversation.


**TLDR:**


-


A hiring manager is a responsibility attached to an existing role, not a job title people apply for.


-


They own role criteria, interviews, and the hiring decision.


-


Recruiters own pipeline, screening, and process coordination.


-


Authority for offers and approvals varies by company, so confirm it at intake.


## What Is a Hiring Manager?


A hiring manager is the person accountable for filling an open role. This is a responsibility attached to an existing management or leadership job, not a standalone position someone applies for. A sales manager, an engineering lead, an operations head, a restaurant owner, or a founder at a small startup can all hold this responsibility alongside their regular duties.


> Hiring manager describes responsibility for a particular hire, not a job title on its own.


This person is often, but not always, the new hire’s future supervisor. A VP of Sales, for example, may be the hiring manager for a salesperson who reports to a director instead. At companies with no recruiter on staff, the hiring manager may also handle sourcing, screening, and scheduling in addition to defining the role and making the selection.


## Hiring Manager Duties and Responsibilities


Hiring managers stay accountable for the hire at every stage, even when a recruiter carries part of the work. Their responsibilities fall into four stages.


### Define the Need and the Criteria


-


Confirm the headcount need and get approval to open the requisition.


-


Define what success looks like in the role, in terms of outcomes the new hire should deliver.


-


Build the job description with the recruiter, separating must-have skills from nice-to-have ones.


### Screen and Interview


-


Review the candidates the recruiter passes along after the first screen.


-


Lead interviews and assess each candidate against the criteria agreed at intake.


-


Check references on finalists.


-


At companies with no recruiter, handle outreach and first screens as well.


### Decide and Close


-


Collect interviewer feedback and compare candidates against the same criteria.


-


Make or recommend the final selection, often pending executive approval.


-


Set offer terms with HR or the recruiter, and negotiate directly when the company expects it.


### Onboard


-


Set expectations for the first 90 days.


-


Introduce the new hire to the team and the work.


-


Check progress early, while problems are still easy to fix.


Authority over compensation, offer approval, and final selection depends on how the company delegates it. Confirm approval limits before making commitments to a candidate.


OPM’s[End-to-End Hiring Roadmap](https://www.opm.gov/policy-data-oversight/human-capital-management/hiring-reform/hiringelements.pdf) assigns federal hiring managers responsibility for reviewing referred candidates, conducting interviews, checking references, and returning the certificate identifying their selection, subject to applicable laws and agency procedures. HR checks minimum qualifications and eligibility, issues the certificate of eligible candidates, and audits the returned certificate for compliance before extending a tentative offer.


## Hiring Manager vs. Recruiter


Recruiters are accountable for the pipeline and the process, while the hiring manager is accountable for the role and the final decision.


Dimension Hiring manager Recruiter


Core question Who can do this job well on my team? Who is qualified and interested, and how do we move them through the process?


Primary focus Role definition and depth of assessment Sourcing, screening, and candidate experience


Owns Criteria, interviews, and selection Pipeline, scheduling, and process coordination


Success measured by Quality of hire and new-hire progress Time to fill, pipeline quality, and candidate experience


Candidate contact Interviews, role expectations, and selling the team Outreach, first screens, logistics, and often offer communication


Decision authority Final selection or recommendation, subject to approvals Screening recommendations and offer support


Relationship to the hire Often the future supervisor Usually none after handoff


A recruiter’s job is to make the hiring manager’s decision a hard one by assembling strong candidates. When none of them fit, the hiring manager sends the recruiter back to rebuild the pool. Indeed’s overview of[hiring manager and recruiter differences](https://www.indeed.com/career-advice/finding-a-job/hiring-manager-vs-recruiter) describes the hiring manager as the person who sets candidate criteria, interviews top candidates, and handles onboarding.


The split shifts by company. A small startup or a retail store may have no recruiter, so the hiring manager does nearly everything. Larger companies with recruiting teams narrow the hiring manager to criteria, interviews, and the decision.


### Hiring Manager vs. HR, Manager, and Supervisor


HR owns employment policy, eligibility checks, and compliance. Manager, line manager, and supervisor describe ongoing oversight of people or work, while hiring manager describes responsibility for one particular hire. Talent acquisition is the broader recruiting function that recruiters sit within.


## How Hiring Managers and Recruiters Work Together


A few habits keep a hiring manager and a recruiter moving together instead of working past each other:


-


**Intake meeting:** agree on role scope, must-haves, timeline, and who owns each step before sourcing starts.


-


**Calibration:** review a handful of sample profiles together so the recruiter learns what a good candidate looks like to the manager.


-


**Job description:** the hiring manager supplies role success criteria and the recruiter shapes the posting; for other roles, follow the[job description guide](https://www.dover.com/blog/job-description-guide) .


-


**Handoffs:** decide upfront who schedules interviews, who sends feedback requests, and who communicates and negotiates the offer.


Trust, and admitting what each side does not know, is what keeps this working.


## Skills of an Effective Hiring Manager


Hiring manager skills should match the work the new hire will do:


-


Functional expertise to judge work samples accurately.


-


Workforce planning that ties headcount requests to actual workload.


-


Structured interviewing to keep questions consistent across candidates.


-


Evidence-based assessment that ties ratings to documented answers.


-


Clear communication to set candidate expectations early.


-


Collaboration with recruiters to keep screening criteria aligned.


-


Legal and ethical judgment, including equal employment rules, job-related questions only, and any company policy on AI use in hiring.


Qualifications come from the underlying management role. No HR degree, recruiting certification, or fixed experience requirement applies universally; training on fair selection, job-related questions, and consistent scoring matters more than credentials.


## How to Become a Hiring Manager


Becoming a hiring manager typically follows greater responsibility within your function, not a move into HR. Build relevant expertise, join interview panels, shadow experienced interviewers, and participate in hiring debriefs before taking on staffing authority. Recruiting and HR careers offer alternative routes, but neither is a prerequisite for departmental hiring; founders weighing outside support can look at[how to choose a startup recruiter](https://www.dover.com/blog/how-to-choose-the-right-recruiter-for-your-startup) .


When searching for hiring manager jobs, look for titles such as engineering manager, sales manager, operations manager, or department head. Check postings for team ownership and authority to hire; the title alone may not confirm either.


## Recruiter Screens and Hiring Manager Interviews


Recruiter screens typically check basic qualifications and expectations;[hiring manager interviews](https://www.dover.com/blog/how-to-interview-candidates-for-your-startup) probe job-specific judgment, execution, and collaboration. Ownership varies by company.


Sample hiring manager interview questions and evidence sought:


-


“Which relevant accomplishment was yours?” Look for personal contribution and results.


-


“How did you choose what to delay?” Listen for priorities and tradeoffs.


-


“A teammate disputes your deadline. What would you do?” Assess planning and collaboration.


Candidates can ask “Who would I report to?”, “What should I accomplish first?”, and “How will you measure my performance?”


## Common Hiring Manager Challenges and Measures of Success


Daily work can crowd out hiring, which is one of several[signs your startup needs a recruiter](https://www.dover.com/blog/signs-startup-hire-recruiter) . Regular recruiting check-ins help flag stalled decisions, while specific working habits tackle recurring problems:


-


Unclear requirements: agree on role scope at intake.


-


Delayed feedback: set deadlines for interview feedback.


-


Inconsistent interviews: use structured scorecards.


-


Disagreements over candidate suitability: name a decision owner.


Track feedback turnaround, stage delays, and offer acceptance, then compare post-hire performance with agreed expectations. Review results with recruiting and HR, since outcomes reflect shared responsibilities.

## FAQs


### Is the hiring manager your boss?


Often yes, but not always. The hiring manager owns the hire, while reporting lines can differ in matrix or shared arrangements. Ask directly who the role reports to rather than assuming from the interview lineup.


### Can a hiring manager also be the recruiter?


Yes. At small companies with no recruiting function, the hiring manager can post the role, source and screen candidates, and schedule interviews, in addition to interviewing and deciding. The workload usually grows with the number of open roles.


### Who negotiates the offer, the recruiter or the hiring manager?


It varies by company. Many have the recruiter handle terms using compensation data, with the hiring manager deciding level and approving the offer, while others have the hiring manager negotiate directly with the candidate. Confirm who owns this step at intake so candidates get a consistent answer.


### Is a hiring manager the same as an HR manager?


No. HR manager is a standing job that oversees policy and compliance across the organization, while hiring manager is a hiring responsibility that any manager can hold for a specific opening. The two roles can coexist on the same hire without overlapping.


### Is hiring manager a job title, and can you apply for one?


No. Hiring manager is a responsibility attached to an existing role, not a standalone position with its own salary. Pay follows the underlying role, such as engineering manager, sales director, or HR manager, and varies by seniority, industry, and location, so benchmark that occupation when you research pay. First-time hiring managers are usually existing managers or senior individual contributors taking on hiring duties, so there is no entry-level hiring manager track.


Postings titled “Hiring Manager” usually turn out to be recruiter, HR, staffing, or ordinary management roles with hiring duties. Read the duties and reporting line to see what the job is. Salary-sharing forums such as Reddit can add context only when the poster names the actual role, seniority, and location.


## Dividing Hiring Work Between Hiring Managers and Recruiters


The hiring manager owns the definition of the role, the depth of candidate assessment, and the final decision. The recruiter owns the pipeline, screening, and coordination that keep candidates moving. HR guards policy and compliance, stepping in when approval rules or legal questions arise. On small teams, one person may carry several of these duties at once, so the practical question is who recommends a candidate, who approves an offer, and who closes the hire, a split that looks different depending on company size and hiring volume. Seen this way, the right division of labor depends less on fixed titles and more on where a team’s hiring process currently stalls.
